content.title: Response to Reviewer 3
content.comment:
We want to thank the reviewer for the time and for the helpful comments. (C- comment, R- Response)
We also want to thank the reviewer for the great score that he/she gave us.

C1 -  Eqn (1), as EMA_t as defined - if "t" indicates time, I feel there is a conflict of this when you use EMA_i; eg EMA_2 is EMA(EMA_1), and recursively one can define EMA_(i+1) = EMA(EMA_i) What is also then EMA without a subscript (i) or (t) ?

R1 - EMA without a script means the operation itself. For example, EMA(EMA1) means the smoothed version of EMA1 - exponential moving average over an exponential moving average. To demonstrate the behavior of different TEMA's components a bit better - we added the right subfigure in Figure 1 

C2 - In Eqn (3) - what is the basis of using these wts - 3, -3, 1? and same in Eqn (2) : 2, -1. The sum of the wts = -1 always - I did not find any discussion or reference on this.

R2 - We understand the point. These wts were actually taken from the original equations of TEMA. We didn't try other options as these were already optimized to some extent when TEMA was initially introduced in the literature. We added this important point to the paper.


C3 - Can one recursively define with higher order ? - say, PEMA - EMA of 5th order, say ?

R3 - In general, there is no limitation and it can be definitely explored. However, currently, in literature only EMA, DEMA and TEMA were introduced and we tested all of them. The TEMA supplied the best results, therefore we used it.

C4 - The analytical proof that TEMA in Eqn (3) enables convergence for the learning process is not given and discussed. An Appendix would have strengthened the paper.

R4 - Similar to our response to Reviewer 4, we agree that this can make the paper a bit stronger, especially from the theoretical side, however, a super important ICLR 2022 blog called "Does Adam Converge and When?" raises key questions about optimizers' convergence. It concludes that the convergence of an optimizer is a much more complex question and a problem-dependent question and not straightforward as it is considered in the literature. It requires much more thorough research for each individual dataset. Therefore, although we agree that such an analysis can enhance our contribution, we still think that it is an issue that should be explored more thoroughly in future dedicated research and that for now, the extensive evaluation that we conducted may fill this theoretical gap. We will definitely explore this aspect later on. 

C5 - Empirical justification of this using gradient variance ratio is acceptable, but not universal. I am concerned of this.

R5 - We agree with the reviewer that it may not be universal enough because it is not theoretical proof. However, our motivation to introduce this part at the end of the script (it is not the focus of the paper) was to show that the known process convergence-gradients variance relationship is valid also for our examples. Even if it is not general enough, it can definitely show promising results in this direction.  

C6 - On what situations will convergence fail? Have you explained, why in table 1 , the process FAME is not superior for Mobilenet and Inception-v3?

R6 - This is a very good comment about an open question that we still have to explore. In the beginning, we thought that it relates to the number of network parameters, but further and deeper investigation should be done.

content.title: Response to Reviewer 4
content.comment:
We want to thank the reviewer for the time and for the helpful comments. (C- comment, R- Response)

C1 -  First of all, many works such as Adam, Adamw extensively conducted convergence analysis. However, in this paper, there seem to be only the experimental results without any convergence analysis. In my view, the optimizer without convergence analysis is hard to be used even though the experimental results are superior to others.

R1 - We agree that some optimization papers present convergence analysis. Adam is an example of that. However, not all papers that present new optimizers do that. We agree that this can make the paper a bit stronger, especially from the theoretical side, however, a super important ICLR 2022 blog called "Does Adam Converge and When?" raises key questions about optimizers' convergence. It concludes that the convergence of an optimizer is a much more complex question and a problem-dependent question and not straightforward as it is considered in the literature. It requires much more thorough research for each individual dataset. Therefore, although we agree that such an analysis can enhance our contribution, we still think that it is an issue that should be explored more thoroughly in future dedicated research and that for now, the extensive evaluation that we conducted may fill this theoretical gap. 

C2 - I don't understand why the authors mention that TEMA is related to stock domain. I think that moving averages can be used in other many fields, not only stock domain. It seems that exploring several properties or analysis of TEMA can be better.

R2 - We agree that moving averages can be used in many fields. The reviewer is absolutely right. We might need to clarify this point a bit more. The main reason to mention the stock domain specifically is that using higher-degree exponential moving averages was not done before in deep learning optimizers - we encountered the TEMA as an indicator and trend predictor only in the stock market domain. In this paper, we wanted to show the contribution of such an approach for performance improvement. 
Regarding explanations about different TEMA's properties - we introduced the motivation and the proposed method, and an intuition of why it works well and better than the original EMA. We also thoroughly explored the different components of TEMA and their individual effect on the overall performance. To do that, we demonstrated their typical behavior as smoothed versions of the original EMA, both in the Related Work explanations and in Figure 1.

C3 - the paper motivation should be clarified better

R3 - We thank the reviewer for this important comment. We clarified it better in the revised paper. 
In this paper, we aim to propose a better optimizer that can track changes in gradients and reduce the lag time (between the real change and the optimizer's prediction) better and faster than current optimizers.
To do that, we introduce FAME optimizer - the first to take advantage of the Triple Exponential Moving Average. Through the use of TEMA, which provides richer information about gradients and their trend, we improve the fundamental block of the commonly-used EMA.

content.title: Response to Reviewer 2
content.comment:
We want to thank the reviewer for the time and for the helpful comments. (C- comment, R- Response)

C1 - Novelty. The novelty is relatively marginal. It brings an existing technique in stock prediction (triple EMA) to DNN optimizer design. This novelty is relatively marginal in ICLR standard.

R1 - We respectfully disagree with the reviewer. Although the reviewer is right that the triple exponential moving average was derived from the financial domain, this is still the first time a higher-order exponential moving average has been applied to deep network optimization. All other current optimizers utilize simple exponential moving averages to update the gradients. Moreover, as we explained in the paper, the way that we apply the triple exponential moving average in our framework is completely different from the way that it is used in the stock market. While in the latter it is used as a simple indicator, here it is used as an integral part of the optimization procedure. 

C2 - Concerns about hyper parameter tuning. This FAME optimizer introduces four more hyper-parameters to tune compared to Adam optimizer. Even though the authors mentioned that the hyper-parameters tuning is quite robust, tuning is still much more complex to be practically used. In addition, the comparisons given in the paper is claimed to be using "optimal hyper-parameters". However the full details of searching range for all experiments are not given. I would recommend the authors to give them in supplementary. Without a double check of the fairness of the hyper-parameter tuning, it is not very convincing to make the claim.

R2 - We want to clarify and give more details about the hyper parameter tuning. As the reviewer mentioned – we showed the robustness of the method performance on different sets of parameters – this means that even if there are a few additional parameters, the overall performance is not sensitive, which makes the hyper-parameters selection not too critical. 
In addition, the details of searching range for the experiments are already given in the original submitted paper.
However, according to the reviewer's comment, we added the remaining details about the other datasets to the revised paper – 
"For CIFAR-100, Cityscapes, MS-COCO and Pascal-VOC, we tested the following range of values for each hyper-parameter - β_3,4,5∈[0,0.8] with discrete steps of 0.1 for each β_and ε∈[0.01,0.1] with increments of 0.01. Applying all these options, the largest difference between the classification accuracies while using different sets of parameters was only 3.72\%. These results support the high robustness of our FAME over different values of hyper-parameters."
	
C3 - Additional memory cost and computational cost. This new optimizer increases steps to compute double EMA and triple EMA during each training step. These values also need to be preserved during training. It thus requires more memory cost and computational cost. The author didn't mention this disadvantage.

R3 - The following description was added to the paper – 
"The proposed optimizer requires a slightly higher memory cost and computational time, compared with other optimizers. For example, compared with Adam, it requires twice the memory and a 5% increase in computational time. Compared with SGD, the equivalent values were 2.5 times in memory cost and 7% in computational time. It is important to clarify, that this increase in both aspects is not critical and can be easily handled by commonly- used hardware."  

C4 - Review summary - "Even though I like that the intuitive idea and extensive experiments, the main concerns are: 1) the novelty is only incremental. 2) the results are not significantly better given that it introduces a lot of new hyper-parameters that need to be tuned and additional memory/computation cost. The benefits of this paper to the research community is not significant enough."

R4 - We hope that by providing more details and responses to your concerns, we will be able to convince you that such a method that applies a Triple EMA for network optimization (for the first time in deep learning) is crucial. By analyzing each component of the TEMA and demonstrating their typical behavior, we were able to present improved results, providing intuition and in-depth analysis for better performance.

content.title: Response to Reviewer 1
content.comment:
We want to thank the reviewer for the time and for the helpful comments. (C- comment, R- Response)	

C1 - There are important baselines [1,2] missing to compare. The performance of [1,2] has been much better than Adam according to their reported results.

R1 - We respectfully disagree with the reviewer. It is important to take the reviewer's attention to all the optimizers we compared. Our method was compared with five different optimizers. We compared our FAME optimizer not only with the extremely popular Adam and SGD optimizers, but also with more recent versions of ADAM, such as AdaGrad, AdaBound, and AdamW. This is a comprehensive comparison with other common optimizers. 
Moreover, the authors of ADAHESSIAN present its performance capabilities in their paper, which are only comparable to AdamW (sometimes a bit better, sometimes a bit worse). Because we present a significant improvement over AdamW, it is reasonable to expect that the same improvement magnitude will apply to AdaHESIAN as well. 
Despite all mentioned above, we will add the comparison to AdaHESSIAN to the paper because we think that any further evaluation may enhance the strengths of the method even more. 

C2 - There is no theoretical support for why the proposed algorithm exhibits better empirical performance than baseline optimizers.

R2 - It is important to clarify - the paper is not a purely theoretical one but this is also the reason to provide such an extensive method validation that we didn't see in other papers (14 architectures, 5 datasets, and comparing with 5 different optimizers). We introduced the motivation and the proposed method, and an intuition of why it works well and better than the original EMA. We also thoroughly explored the different components of TEMA and their individual effect on the overall performance. To do that, we demonstrated their typical behavior as smoothed versions of the original EMA, both in the Related Work explanations and in Figure 1. In addition, we presented an extensive in-depth validation to convince the reader about the strengths and abilities of the method. We tested our method on 5 different public benchmarks, 14 different architectures and compared with 5 different optimizers. To the best of our knowledge, this is a super-extensive validation even when compared to non-theoretical papers.    

C3 - Missing experiments on the large-scale dataset, like ImageNet.

R3 - We agree with the reviewer. This is primarily due to computational load and time. It is because training from scratch is the best way to evaluate the contributions of a new optimizer. It is impossible to demonstrate the pure effect of the new optimizer on a pretrained model that was previously trained with another optimizer. In order to train ImageNet from scratch, a lot of computation time and resources will be required. However, our optimizer was still tested on 5 publicly available benchmarks (fair ones, not easy ones like MNIST or SVHN) in order to prove its strengths and capabilities. Many papers use these benchmarks without analyzing ImageNet (due to the computational limitations we mentioned). Furthermore, we observed that most other papers do not analyze five different datasets, but only two to three.  

C4 - The technical contributions of this paper are marginal. Applying FEMA to deep learning seems simple without in-depth analysis and comprehensive study.

R4 - We respectfully disagree with the reviewer. This is the first time presenting a higher-order exponential moving average for deep network optimization. All other current optimizers utilize simple moving averages to update the gradients. Moreover, as we explained in the paper, the way that we applied the triple exponential moving average in our framework is completely different than the way that it is used in the stock market. While in the latter it is used as a simple indicator, here it is used as an integral part of the optimization procedure. Also, as we explained in our response to comment 2 - we supplied the intuition of why it works well and better than the original EMA. We also thoroughly explored the different components of TEMA and their individual effect on the overall performance. To do that, we demonstrated their typical behavior as smoothed versions of the original EMA, both in the Related Work explanations and in Figure 1.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper invents a new method for optimization inspired by other areas. The proposed Triple Exponential Moving Average (FEMA) utilized multi-level trend estimators commonly applied in the stock market. Compared with the standard EMA, the FEMA considers the changes in the moving average of the original data, which is supposed to be helpful for model optimization towards smother or more global optima. Such proposed FEMA is verified on multiple benchmarks with promising results against many baseline methods.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Pros: 
+  The paper is generally clear and easy to follow.

+ The idea is somewhat novel. This is the first attempt to apply FEMA to deep learning. 

+ The motivation for incorporating high-order EMA for smoother optimization is reasonable.

Cons:
- There are important baselines [1,2] missing to compare. The performance of [1,2] has been much better than Adam according to their reported results.

- There is no theoretical support for why the proposed algorithm exhibits better empirical performance than baseline optimizers.

- Missing experiments on the large-scale dataset, like ImageNet.

- The technical contributions of this paper are marginal. Applying FEMA to deep learning seems simple without in-depth analysis and comprehensive study.

References

[1] Zhuang et al. AdaBelief Optimizer: Adapting Stepsizes by the Belief in Observed Gradients. NeurIPS 2020

[2] Yao et al. ADAHESSIAN: An Adaptive Second Order Optimizer for Machine Learning. AAAI 2021

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes to use Triple Exponential Moving Average (TEMA) in optimizer update (i.e. the FAME optimizer). It replaces the original mt and vt in Adam-like optimizer with <mt, mt(mt), mt(mt(mt))> and <vt, vt(vt), vt(vt(vt))>. This optimizer is evaluated on 5 datasets, 14 architectures to demonstrate that it can achieve similar or better performance compared to prior work on optimizers.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength: 

1. Thourough experiments. To evaluate the optimization quality of the optimizer, the authors did extensive experiments on 5 datasets and 14 architectures. The author also compared with multiple prior work optimizers.The results are supportive of the claim that this optimizer can perform similar or better than previous optimizers.

2. Idea is simple and intuitive. This paper introduces the idea of triple EMA from stock prediction to DNN optimization. It makes relatively simple change to existing optimizer and is easy to implement.

Weakness: 
1. Novelty. The novelty is relatively marginal. It brings an existing technique in stock prediction (triple EMA) to DNN optimizer design. This novelty is relatively marginal in ICLR standard.
  
2. Concerns about hyper parameter tuning. This FAME optimizer introduces four more hyper-parameters to tune compared to Adam optimizer. Even though the authors mentioned that the hyper-parameters tuning is quite robust, tuning is still much more complex to be pratically used. In addition, the comparisons given in the paper is claimed to be using "optimal hyper-parameters". However the full details of searching range for all experiments are not given. I would recommend the authors to give them in supplementary. Without a double check of the fairness of the hyper-parameter tuning, it is not very convincing to make the claim.

3. Additional memory cost and computational cost. This new optimizer increases steps to compute double EMA and triple EMA during each training step. These values also need to be preserved during training. It thus requires more memory cost and computational cost. The author didn't mention this disadvantage.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
- The overall paper is written with quite good clarity, except the part regarding hyper-parameters tuning (the weakness mentioned above). 
- This paper should be reproducible if the configs for all optimizers are given on all of the datasets/architectures. Currently it is not clearly given in the paper or supplementary.
- Novelty of this paper is only marginal (see above weakness).
content.summary_of_the_review:
Even though I like that the intuitive idea and extensive experiments, I would still recommend not accepting the paper with the current shape. The main concerns are: 1) the novelty is only incremental. 2) the results are not significantly better given that it introduces a lot of new hyper-parameters that need to be tuned and additional memory/computation cost. The benefits of this paper to the research community is not significant enough.

----
after rebuttal, some concerns are addressed. However the new arguments do not fully convince me, especially the marginal novelty part (I don't mean no novelty, just marginal). So I adjust the score to be 5.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper propose a DL optimizer based on the Triple Exponential Moving Average (TEMA), a technical indicator
which adds richer multi-level information about data changes and trends compared to the simple Exponential Moving
Average, where the gradients moments are better estimated.

Extensive experiments shown using 5 benchmarks (CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, PASCAL-VOC,
MS-COCO and Cityscapes) to test the method, over 14 different
learning architectures, 5 different optimizers, and various vision tasks (detection,
segmentation, and classification). The paper claims that the results clearly indicate that the robustness
and accuracy of FAME optimizer are superior over others.

Contributions are: (i) formulating  TEMA, from an earlier EMA model, used in stock market predictions;
(ii) Extensive experiments to ascertain the success of TEMA on various benchmarks and Vision tasks.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Major contribution is the crisp formulation of TEMA model, from gradient moments.
Although it combines EMA and ADAM based principles, I believe that this will pave way for a good amount
of research in  this direction.
I am convinced with the results in Figs. 2-5 and Tables 1-4.

I have a few issues though:

In Eqn (1),  as EMA_t as defined -   if "t" indicates time, I feel there is a conflict of this
when you use EMA_i;
eg EMA_2 is EMA(EMA_1), and recursively one can define EMA_(i+1)  = EMA(EMA_i)
What is also then EMA without a subscript (i) or (t) ?

In Eqn (3) - what is basis of using these wts - 3, -3, 1?
and same in Eqn (2) : 2, -1.
The sum of the wts = -1 always - I did not find any discussion or reference on this.

Can one recursively define with higher order ? - say, PEMA - EMA of 5th order, say ?

The analytical proof that TEMA in Eqn (3) enables convergence for the learning process is not given and discussed.
An Appendix would have strengthened the paper.

Empirical justification of this using gradient variance ratio is acceptable, but not universal.
I am concerned of this.

On what situations will convergence fail?

Have you explained, why in table 1 , the process FAME is not superior for Mobilenet and Inception-v3?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper was quite easy to read. The analytics were almost clearly drafted. 
Quality is as expected for ICLR level.

The idea although not quite novel by itself, may still be considered as quite significant.

Although not verified, but it appears that the material and results are reproducible.
content.summary_of_the_review:
Inspite of a few concerns expressed in above, I am willing to accept the paper,
if other reviewers also feel so.

Extensive experiments and detailed  analytics are acceptable.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper "FAME: Fast adaptive moment estimation based on triple exponential moving average" proposes an optimizer incorporating TEMA, which is a technical indicator in stock market domain. The authors mention that TEMA can provide richer information about gradients and their trends when using it for optimizers, so that they construct an optimizer in this paper. The experimental results show that the proposed model can achieve superior performance than others.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength 
As the authors discuss TEMA intuitively, TEMA can have richer information such as 2nd derivative of the data in a rough sense. Applying TEMA to optimizers seems to be quite novel because it has more delicate information to find an optimal point. The experimental results support their argument.

Weakness
First of all, many works such as Adam, Adamw extensively conducted convergence analysis. However, in this paper, there seem to be only the experimental results without any convergence analysis. In my view, the optimizer without convergence analysis is hard to be used even though the experimental results are superior to others. 

I don't understand why the authors mention that TEMA is related to stock domain. I think that moving averages can be used in other many fields, not only stock domain. It seems that exploring several properties or analysis of TEMA can be better.

(Minor) There seem to be several typo. For example, in algorithm 1, theta hat is. The reviewer expects that the authors check such things.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: As the author mention that TEMA can have richer information, using TEMA for optimizers is OK and it can be novel. However, firstly, the motivation of this paper is not clear for me. What are the limitations of previous methods? Why the proposed model can have outperforming performance in mathematical sense? I think that there needs to be such analysis.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, applying TEMA to optimizers as proposed in the paper can be significant since TEMA can have richer information. And the experimental results show that the proposed model outperforms other models including Adam, Adamw, etc. Superior performance can be significant and the idea of using TEMA can be novel. However, there are no convergence analysis and likely several improper paragraphs in the paper. Moreover, the motivation of this paper isn't clear to me. If there are rigorous convergence analysis and clear motivations, it will be better than now.

content.title: FAME: Fast Adaptive Moment Estimation based on Triple Exponential Moving Average
content.TL;DR: We propose the first optimizer that is based on the Triple Exponential Moving Average for deep learning
content.abstract: Network optimization is a key step in deep learning, which broadly impacts different domains (e.g. natural language, computer vision). Over the years, several optimizers have been developed - some are adaptive and converge quickly, while others are not adaptive but may be more accurate. However, due to the fact that most current optimizers' use simple Exponential Moving Average, gradient trends and their rapid changes may not be accurately identified, resulting in sub-optimal network performance. In this paper, we propose the first deep optimizer based on the Triple Exponential Moving Average (TEMA), a technical indicator originally developed to predict stock market trends. TEMA adds richer multi-level information about data changes and trends compared to the simple Exponential Moving Average. As a result, the gradients moments are better estimated. Furthermore, instead of using TEMA in the same way as the stock domain, here we use it as part of a continuous average during an optimization procedure. We extensively validated our method. Five benchmarks (CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, PASCAL-VOC, MS-COCO, and Cityscapes) were used to test our method, as well as 14 different learning architectures, five different optimizers, and various vision tasks (detection, segmentation, and classification). The results clearly indicate that the robustness and accuracy of our FAME optimizer are superior to those of others.
